How is property tax run in New Mexico?

New Mexico property tax is a county-level system overseen by the state Taxation and Revenue Department. The county assessor sets the value, the county treasurer collects the tax, and the Property Tax Division at the state department supports the counties and runs the collection process for long-delinquent accounts.

The state has 33 counties, and delinquent auctions are not held in all of them each year. The constitution caps the percentage of value that tax rates apply to at thirty-three and one-third percent, so the net taxable value on your notice is a fraction of market value. A separate limit in the Property Tax Code slows annual increases on homes, described below.

For a seller, three dates and one lien do most of the work: the notice of valuation in spring, the two tax installments, the January 1 lien date and the closing statement that settles what is owed.

What dates and numbers matter most?

Most New Mexico homeowners need only a handful of figures, and each one below comes from the statute or agency page named.

ItemRuleSource
Notice of valuationMailed by the assessor around April 1NMSA 7-38-20
Protest petitionFiled with the assessor, generally thirty days after the notice is mailedNMSA 7-38-24
Tax installmentsNovember 10 and April 10, in two equal installments for bills of $10 or moreNMSA 7-38-38
Interest on unpaid taxOne percent a month, starting thirty days after the due dateNMSA 7-38-49
Tax lienAttaches to real property from January 1 of the tax yearNMSA 7-38-48
Residential value limitHigher of 103 percent of prior year value or 106.1 percent of value two years backNMSA 7-36-21.2
Head of family exemptionUp to $2,000 of taxable valueNMSA 7-37-4
Veteran exemption$10,000, adjusted annually for inflationNM TRD release, Aug. 2026

Interest does not run on interest or on penalties, and it accrues even while a protest is pending. If the protest succeeds, interest is computed on the unpaid tax finally found due.

How does the cap on increases work, and what resets it?

A home's taxable value cannot rise in a year by more than the higher of 103 percent of the prior year's value or 106.1 percent of the value two years earlier. The cap protects a long-time owner from sudden jumps in the market.

The cap does not apply in the first tax year a property is valued, to physical improvements (other than solar installations), to a change in use or zoning, or in the tax year after a change of ownership. After a sale, the county values the house at its current and correct value under Section 7-36-21.2.

Some transfers are not a change of ownership. The list includes transfers between spouses, to a revocable trust for the owner, spouse or child, and to a child who lives in the home as a principal residence. A transfer between a person and an LLC they own is a change of ownership, according to a 2019 Court of Appeals decision.

The takeaway for sellers is that your tax bill and the buyer's bill can differ. An estimate of carrying costs should use the reset value, not your old bill.

Which exemptions can lower a New Mexico tax bill?

The head of family exemption takes up to $2,000 off taxable value for qualifying residents, and the veteran exemption now takes $10,000. Both are deducted from taxable value to reach net taxable value.

  • Head of family: available to a married person, widow or widower, a head of household supporting a related person, a single person or a condominium association member who pays tax through the association. Only one person in a household qualifies, and the exemption can be claimed in only one county per year.
  • Veteran: the standard exemption rose from $4,000 to $10,000, and the state reported it saved 65,720 veterans an estimated $19 million in 2025. Veterans get a certificate of eligibility from the Department of Veterans' Services and file it with the county assessor.
  • Disabled veteran: from 2026, partially disabled veterans can receive a prorated exemption by disability rating, and 7,096 did from March through June 2026.
  • Valuation freeze: a single-family home owned and occupied by someone 65 or older, or disabled, with prior-year modified gross income at or under $35,000 as adjusted for inflation, is limited to its assessed value in the year the owner qualifies.

Under Section 7-38-17, exemptions must be claimed within thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed and then continue automatically if nothing changes. A change in eligibility or ownership must be reported to the assessor by the last day of February of the following year. A knowing false claim is a misdemeanor.

How do you protest a valuation?

File a written petition with the county assessor, generally within thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed. The petition must give your name, the property description, why you think the value is wrong and what you believe is correct.

The assessor may offer an informal conference first, and the Taxation and Revenue Department encourages one because many protests are resolved there. If not, a three-member county valuation protests board hears the case. The board is independent of the assessor and includes two county residents appointed by the commission and an appraisal officer from the state Property Tax Division.

  • The assessor schedules the hearing and mails notice at least fifteen days before it, though discovery requests can take thirty days to answer, so start preparing early.
  • The assessor's value is presumed correct, and the owner carries the burden of presenting evidence to overcome that presumption.
  • Testimony is under oath and a verbatim record is made.
  • The board issues a written order within thirty days of the hearing, and all protests are to be decided within 180 days of filing.
  • An appeal goes to district court within thirty days of the board's order.

A second route exists after payment. An owner who pays the tax before the delinquency date can protest value, classification or a denied exemption by filing a claim for refund in district court under Section 7-38-39.

What happens when property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid tax accrues interest at one percent a month from thirty days after the due date, and the lien stays on the property until it is paid. The lien is a first lien and paramount to any other interest, perfected or not. It arises by operation of law and does not depend on a recorded notice.

The state's Delinquent Property Tax Bureau pursues collection at the end of the third full year of delinquency. Sales are held annually as title research is completed, usually at the county courthouse, and the state does not hold sales in all 33 counties each year. The department's auction page listed a sale in San Miguel County on November 19, 2026.

Several rules from the department's FAQ affect owners facing a sale.

  • The minimum bid is the total of taxes, penalty, interest and costs due.
  • The state issues a tax deed equivalent to a quitclaim deed, sold as is with no warranty of title.
  • The sale extinguishes the tax lien only. No other liens are extinguished.
  • New Mexico has no right of redemption for former owners, only a two-year period to challenge the sale in court under Section 7-38-70.
  • A 120-day federal IRS redemption period may apply if the federal government holds a lien.
  • County treasurers can seize and sell a mobile home for delinquent tax under Section 7-38-53.

Because there is no redemption right, selling before the auction is the main way for an owner to keep any equity.

How do you sell a New Mexico house with tax due?

Sellers can pay back tax from the sale proceeds at closing, because the tax is a first lien that stays on the property until it is paid. The practical steps are short.

  • Ask the county treasurer for the current balance, including interest, before you list.
  • Check whether a head of family or veteran exemption was ever claimed, because exemptions must be claimed within thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed.
  • Tell the assessor by the end of February after you sell if you lose an exemption.
  • Confirm there is no pending protest you want to preserve, and remember interest runs during a protest.
  • Ask the title company for a payoff figure that includes the November and April installments for the year of closing.

Cash Home Buyers buys New Mexico houses as they are, including homes with back taxes owed, and the closing statement handles the payoff. We are not a tax advisor, so confirm balances with the treasurer and the Property Tax Division at (505) 827-0883.

More questions about New Mexico Property Tax Guide

When are New Mexico property taxes due?

In two equal installments, November 10 and April 10, for bills of $10 or more. Interest of one percent a month begins thirty days after each due date if the installment is not paid.

How long do I have to protest my New Mexico property valuation?

Generally thirty days after the assessor mails the notice of valuation. The petition goes to the county assessor, who schedules a hearing before the county valuation protests board.

Does New Mexico cap how much my property tax value can rise?

Yes, for residential property. The value cannot exceed the higher of 103 percent of the prior year or 106.1 percent of the value two years earlier. The cap resets after a change of ownership.

Can I get my house back after a New Mexico tax auction?

The state says it has no right of redemption for former owners. A former owner has two years to challenge the sale in court under Section 7-38-70, and a 120-day federal redemption period applies if the IRS holds a lien.

What is the New Mexico veteran property tax exemption?

The standard exemption for veterans who own property rose from $4,000 to $10,000, adjusted annually for inflation. Veterans get a certificate of eligibility from the Department of Veterans' Services and file it with the county assessor.

title: New Mexico Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

New Mexico Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Mexico Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the New Mexico Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Mexico House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Mexico?
We buy New Mexico houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What is the New Mexico homestead exemption?

The New Mexico homestead exemption is a creditor protection rule in Section 42-10-9 NMSA 1978. It shields part of the value of your primary residence from a judgment creditor, from a bankruptcy trustee and from probate administrators.

Many owners confuse it with property tax relief. The two programs are separate. This page covers the creditor protection first, then explains the tax exemptions that sometimes share the "homestead" label, because the difference matters when you are deciding how and when to sell.

The statute says a person has a homestead exemption in a domicile or land the person owns and uses as a primary residence. The protection runs against attachment, execution or foreclosure by a judgment creditor. It does not protect the property against a mortgage you signed.

How much is the exemption, and when did it change?

The current amount is $150,000, or $300,000 in one situation: the claimant's spouse died within two years before the claim and the spouse could have claimed the exemption had they lived. The amount comes from the 2023 amendment, which took effect July 1, 2023 and applies to actions filed on or after that date.

The history in the annotations shows how much the number has moved.

PeriodHomestead amountSource detail
Before 1993$20,000Raised to $30,000 by the 1993 amendment
1993 to 2007$30,000Raised to $60,000 effective June 15, 2007
2007 to mid 2023$60,000 per ownerEach joint owner of a jointly owned homestead had a separate $60,000
Actions filed on or after July 1, 2023$150,000$300,000 for a spouse who died within two years before the claim

An older court case noted in the annotations holds that a legislative increase cannot be claimed against a judgment lien that attached before the increase took effect. If a lien is old, the amount in force when it attached can matter.

What counts as a domicile under the statute?

A domicile is any shelter or dwelling you use as a primary residence, and the statute lists a mobile home, trailer, recreational vehicle or outbuilding as examples. It applies even if the dwelling does not meet building or housing regulations.

Subsection D says the section is to be construed liberally in favor of the person claiming it. Court decisions collected under the statute give a sense of how that plays out.

  • An equitable owner, such as a buyer under a contract, can claim the exemption, not only the holder of a recorded deed.
  • A debtor who held a life estate in her residence was allowed to claim it in a 2020 federal bankruptcy decision.
  • A debtor with an undivided quarter interest in an inherited house still titled in his deceased parents' names was allowed to claim it in another 2020 bankruptcy decision, because title passes to heirs at death under the Uniform Probate Code.
  • A trailer used as a dwelling qualified, and two rental trailers on the same lot did not defeat the claim.
  • A debtor who moved out because creditors had taken judgments did not abandon the homestead when she intended to return.

These are bankruptcy and appellate rulings applied to their own facts. They show direction, not a guarantee for your situation.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the exemption does not protect

The exemption does not apply to garnishment or to properly perfected liens of secured creditors, so a recorded mortgage or deed of trust is untouched by it. Subsection E of the statute says so directly.

Several other limits come up often in the annotated cases.

  • A mortgage can waive the exemption. An old Supreme Court case holds that an owner can give it up by mortgage or other act.
  • Sale proceeds are a gray area. A 1991 bankruptcy decision held that when an owner voluntarily sells the homestead, the proceeds are not exempt.
  • Intentional damage to the property can carry an equitable lien against the exemption, as in a foreclosure where the debtor sabotaged the house.
  • Property tax is a first lien on real property from January 1 of the tax year under Section 7-38-48, ahead of other interests, and the homestead exemption is a protection against judgment creditors, not against that lien.

A judgment lien still attaches to a home. A 2019 bankruptcy decision held that a judgment lien encumbers the homestead and can be avoided to the extent it impairs the exemption. The exemption limits what a creditor can collect. It does not keep the lien from showing up on title.

How do you claim it?

You claim the exemption in the proceeding where a creditor is trying to collect, using the court forms for that proceeding. The statute's cross references point to Rule 4-803 NMRA for a claim of exemptions on execution and Rule 4-808A for the notice of the right to claim exemptions.

In a foreclosure, an answer is the place to assert it. A 1998 Court of Appeals decision allowed a mortgagor to keep the exemption against a junior judgment lien because she raised it in her answer and obtained court approval of a sale to a third party while the case was pending. An older Supreme Court decision denied the exemption to mortgagors who failed to assert it against junior lienholders in their answers.

One practical warning: a court notice form posted on the New Mexico Courts site in late 2023 still showed the old $60,000 figure. Check the current text of the statute, not only the form, before relying on a number.

Homestead exemption versus property tax exemptions

The property tax exemptions are a different set of rules, and they reduce a county tax bill instead of protecting equity from creditors. The three that most homeowners ask about are listed below.

ProgramWhat it doesWho it covers
Head of family exemption (7-37-4)Up to $2,000 off the taxable value of residential propertyA New Mexico resident who is a married person, widow or widower, head of household supporting a related person, single person or condominium association member; one claim per household and one county per year
Veteran exemptionRaised from $4,000 to $10,000, adjusted annually for inflationVeterans who own property; certificate of eligibility from the Department of Veterans' Services, filed with the county assessor
Valuation freeze (7-36-21.3)Caps the assessed value of a single-family homeOwner-occupants aged 65 or older, or disabled, whose prior-year modified gross income did not exceed $35,000 as adjusted for inflation

Under Section 7-38-17, head of family and veteran exemptions continue automatically once allowed if nothing changes. A first claim is due within thirty days after the assessor mails the notice of valuation. If you lose eligibility, including by selling, you must tell the county assessor by the last day of February of the following year. A knowing false claim is a misdemeanor with a fine up to $1,000.

An August 2026 state release said that 7,096 partially disabled veterans received prorated exemptions from March through June 2026, the first year all disabled veterans could claim one on a primary residence.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens to your tax benefits when you sell?

A sale ends your eligibility for the head of family, veteran and valuation freeze benefits on that house, and the buyer's value is reset. Under Section 7-36-21.2, the three percent annual cap on residential value increases does not apply in the tax year after a change of ownership. The county values the home at current and correct value that year.

That matters for pricing the sale and for what the buyer pays afterward. A house you have owned for many years with a capped value can be reassessed upward for the new owner, even though your own bill was low.

Property tax is payable in two installments, November 10 and April 10, under Section 7-38-38. Unpaid tax draws interest of one percent a month starting thirty days after the due date.

Selling a New Mexico home when creditors or liens are involved

If a judgment lien or unpaid debt is attached to your house, selling can be the cleanest way to deal with it, but the order of payment matters. Liens are paid from proceeds at closing in the order the title company finds them.

  • Pull a title report early so you know every recorded lien and its amount.
  • Confirm whether a judgment lien attached before July 1, 2023, since the exemption amount in force at that time may apply.
  • Ask a New Mexico attorney whether a claim of exemption should be filed before closing, particularly if a creditor has started execution.
  • Keep the property tax installments current so no tax lien rides along with the sale.
  • If the home is inherited and still in a deceased parent's name, resolve who has authority to sign before listing.

Cash Home Buyers works with owners in these situations and buys houses as they are, so repairs and showings are not part of the timeline. We are not a law firm, and nothing here replaces advice from a lawyer who knows your case.

More questions about New Mexico Homestead Exemption

How much is the New Mexico homestead exemption in 2026?

It is $150,000, or $300,000 if the claimant's spouse died within two years before the claim and could have claimed it. The figures come from Section 42-10-9 as amended in 2023, effective July 1, 2023 for actions filed on or after that date.

Does the homestead exemption stop a mortgage foreclosure?

No. Subsection E of the statute says it does not apply to properly perfected liens of secured creditors or to garnishment. A mortgage you signed stays enforceable.

Do I have to apply to the county for the homestead exemption?

No. You assert it in the court case where a creditor is collecting, using the claim of exemption forms or your answer in a foreclosure. The county programs that reduce tax, such as head of family, are claimed with the assessor instead.

Are sale proceeds protected after I sell my home?

Not reliably. A 1991 bankruptcy decision noted in the annotations held that proceeds of a voluntary sale are not exempt. Talk to an attorney before a sale if a creditor is pursuing you.

Can I claim the exemption on an inherited house?

Possibly. A 2020 bankruptcy decision allowed the exemption for an heir's undivided interest in an inherited house still titled in the deceased parents' names. The result depended on the heir's ownership interest and occupancy, so it is not automatic.

title: New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in New Mexico
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Mexico House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Mexico?
We buy New Mexico houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does New Mexico charge an estate tax?

In practice, no. The state's Taxation and Revenue Department says New Mexico's estate tax was phased out because of federal tax law changes as of January 1, 2005. The Estate Tax Act, Section 7-7-1 NMSA 1978 and following, is still on the books, and the department still asks for paperwork in one situation.

If the estate has to file the federal estate tax return, Form 706, for any reason, the personal representative also files a New Mexico return, form RPD-41058. When the department receives both, it issues a certificate of no tax due for the estate's records. The state due date is the federal due date, including any extension of time for the federal return.

The department describes the state tax as equal to the federal credit on the net estate. Returns and payments go to the New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department, P.O. Box 25123, Santa Fe, NM 87504-5123. For help, call (505) 827-0763 or email Other.Taxes@tax.nm.gov.

Does New Mexico have an inheritance tax?

No. The department states plainly that New Mexico does not impose an inheritance tax, and the Tax Foundation's state profile says the same: New Mexico has neither an estate tax nor an inheritance tax. Heirs who receive a house, cash or other property do not owe the state a tax for receiving it.

That puts New Mexico apart from states that tax the heir, such as Kentucky, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, the five the Tax Foundation lists.

When does the federal estate tax apply?

Federal estate tax applies only when the estate is large. For people who die in 2026, the IRS lists the basic exclusion amount at $15,000,000, which equals a credit of $5,945,800 at 2026 rates. Most estates fall far below that line.

The IRS says the estate tax return is due nine months after the date of death. A return can also be filed when no tax is owed, for example to elect portability of a deceased spouse's unused exclusion.

TaxDoes it apply to a New Mexico heir selling a house?
New Mexico estate taxPhased out as of January 1, 2005; a no-tax-due certificate is issued if a Form 706 was required
New Mexico inheritance taxNone
Federal estate taxOnly for estates above the exclusion, $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths
Income tax on estate earningsYes, if the estate or trust earns income; filed on form FID-1
Property taxYes; bills continue, and the lien runs from January 1
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What income tax does a New Mexico estate pay?

An estate pays income tax on what it earns while it is open, at personal income tax rates. The state's fiduciary income tax return is form FID-1. The department notes that this is a different tax from the estate tax, because it is based on income the estate or trust generates rather than on the value of what the decedent left.

A house sale during administration can generate gain. Keep the settlement statement, the date-of-death value and a record of repair and carrying costs, because the estate's accountant will need them.

Will heirs owe tax on gain when they sell an inherited house?

Often very little, because inherited property generally takes a new basis. The IRS says the basis of property inherited from a decedent is generally its fair market value on the date of death, whether or not an estate tax return was filed. If you sell for about that value, there is little or no gain to report.

The IRS's basis publication adds a rule for estates that must file Form 706: the basis has to be consistent with the value finally reported for estate tax purposes. If you never receive a statement of that value, your basis can be the appraised value at death used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.

  • Order a date-of-death appraisal early, before repairs or cleanup change the condition.
  • Keep the death certificate, letters from the court, and the deed or tax record showing how title was held.
  • Tell the accountant if you or your spouse gave the property to the decedent within one year before death, because the IRS applies a different basis rule in that case.

Do heirs in New Mexico have to go through probate to sell a house?

Usually yes, unless the house passes outside probate. The New Mexico Courts self-help guide says probate is needed when property is titled in the decedent's name, and not needed for real estate held as joint tenants or with a recorded transfer on death deed.

The small-estate shortcut does not help with a house. A small estate is one worth under $50,000 that includes no real property, so an estate with a house cannot use the affidavit. There is one narrow exception: the primary residence can pass to a surviving spouse by affidavit under Section 45-3-1205 if at least six months have passed, no probate has been filed, and the home's assessed value does not exceed $500,000, among other conditions. That affidavit is filed with the county clerk where the home sits.

Otherwise the case is filed in probate court in the county where the decedent lived. The guide lists a $30 filing cost in probate court, a window from 5 days to 3 years after death, and a possible personal representative's deed to move title. It also says a probate may be opened after three years solely to transfer title to heirs.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How does an inheritance affect the property tax bill?

Property tax continues through probate and can rise afterward. Taxes on real property are a lien from January 1 of the tax year, a first lien that is paramount to other interests. The lien does not depend on a filing, so an old, unpaid bill does not disappear when the owner dies.

The residential valuation cap is 3 percent a year, but it resets after a change of ownership. The statute lists exceptions that matter in an estate: a transfer to a surviving spouse, a transfer to a child who occupies the home as a principal residence, and transfers to or from certain revocable trusts. If the heir who lives there stops qualifying for the head of household exemption, a change of ownership is deemed to occur in the first tax year after that.

A sale to an outside buyer is a change of ownership, so the buyer's value resets. New Mexico's tax dates are November 10 and April 10, with interest after December 10 and May 10.

What should heirs check before listing an inherited New Mexico house?

Confirm who has legal authority to sign, then confirm the tax status of the property. In order:

  • Get letters from the probate court, or confirm a recorded transfer on death deed or joint tenancy.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the current balance, including any unpaid prior-year bill.
  • Ask the accountant whether a Form 706 or a state RPD-41058 is required.
  • Record any deed with the county clerk, since an unrecorded deed does not affect title against a later purchaser.

Call the clerk and treasurer in the county where the house sits. Our county pages for Eddy and McKinley counties list office details.

More questions about New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does New Mexico have an estate tax in 2026?

Effectively no. The state estate tax was phased out as of January 1, 2005. If a federal Form 706 is required, the estate also files form RPD-41058 and receives a certificate of no tax due.

Does New Mexico have an inheritance tax?

No. The Taxation and Revenue Department states that New Mexico does not impose an inheritance tax.

What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?

The IRS lists the basic exclusion amount for 2026 deaths at $15,000,000. The return is due nine months after the date of death.

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house in New Mexico?

Usually, unless the house passed by joint tenancy or a recorded transfer on death deed. The small-estate affidavit does not cover real property, with a narrow spousal exception for a primary residence of $500,000 or less.

What is my tax basis in an inherited house?

Generally the fair market value on the date of death, according to the IRS. A date-of-death appraisal is the usual proof.

Who do I contact about a New Mexico estate tax return?

Call the Taxation and Revenue Department at (505) 827-0763 or email Other.Taxes@tax.nm.gov. Mail returns to P.O. Box 25123, Santa Fe, NM 87504-5123.

Cash Home Buyers in New Mexico

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Mexico?

What does a New Mexico quitclaim deed actually do?

A New Mexico quitclaim deed passes whatever interest the signer holds in a piece of real estate, and the statutory form promises nothing beyond that. Section 47-1-44 NMSA 1978 prints the short forms used for conveyances in the state. The warranty deed form ends with the words "with warranty covenants." The quitclaim form has no such line.

The quitclaim form reads, in outline: for consideration paid, the grantor quitclaims to the grantee, whose address is stated, the described real estate in a named county in New Mexico. A legal description follows, then the witness and seal line, then a place to add the acknowledgment. You can read the forms in the statute text on Justia.

That gap in wording matters when a house is being sold. A seller who signs a quitclaim is not promising that the title is clean, that nobody else owns a share, or that old liens were paid. The buyer receives the seller's interest and carries the risk of everything else. Quitclaim deeds therefore show up most often between relatives, after a divorce, when a name is added or removed, and when a boundary or a gap in the record needs to be cleaned up.

The Santa Fe County Clerk makes a related point from the recording desk. Its office says it is not bonded to tell anyone whether a warranty deed, a special warranty deed or a quitclaim deed is the right form, and it suggests asking a real estate attorney.

How is a quitclaim deed recorded in New Mexico, and what does it cost?

The signed deed goes to the county clerk of the county where the property sits, and the statutory recording fee is $25 per document. Section 14-8-15 NMSA 1978 says a clerk may not accept an instrument for filing until the fees are paid. It also adds $25 for each extra block of ten or fewer entries to the county recording index once a document has more than ten entries. Of each $25 fee, $18 goes to the county general fund and $7 to the clerk's recording and filing fund.

Counties set their own handling rules on top of that. The table below pulls together what the statute and the Santa Fe County Clerk's recording page say.

ItemWhat the source saysSource
Base recording fee$25 for each document filed or recorded14-8-15 NMSA 1978
Large documentsAnother $25 for each added block of ten or fewer index entries beyond the first ten14-8-15 NMSA 1978
SignaturesSanta Fe County asks for the original signature and the notary's original signatureSanta Fe County Clerk
Notary blockMust be on the document, with a legible seal that does not sit over signatures or printed textSanta Fe County Clerk
Electronic filingAvailable through Simplifile or CSC, which charge a convenience fee on top of recording feesSanta Fe County Clerk

Other counties may run things differently, so call the clerk in the county where the house is. The Santa Fe County recording page is a good model of what to expect.

Who has to sign a quitclaim deed on a married couple's house?

Both spouses must sign in most cases. Section 40-3-13 NMSA 1978 says spouses must join in transfers of community real property, and in transfers of separate real property that they own together as joint tenants or tenants in common. A transfer attempted by one spouse alone in violation of that rule is void, with one exception: either spouse may transfer directly to the other without the other joining.

The statute leaves two doors open. A spouse can sign alone under a validly executed and recorded power of attorney, and a spouse who did not join can later ratify the instrument in writing. Separate property owned by only one spouse can generally be transferred without the other's joinder.

For a seller the practical lesson is simple. If you are married and the house was bought during the marriage, plan on both signatures.

What happens if a quitclaim deed is never recorded?

An unrecorded deed still binds the two people who signed it, but it can lose to a later buyer who did not know about it. Section 14-9-3 NMSA 1978 says an unrecorded deed does not affect the title or rights of a purchaser, a good faith mortgagee or a judgment lien creditor who had no knowledge of the unrecorded instrument.

The annotations spell out the consequences:

  • A deed that is not recorded is good between grantor and grantee, and it divests the grantor's title as between them.
  • In one quiet title case, a buyer who purchased in good faith, for value and without knowledge of an earlier unrecorded deed won, even though the buyer's own paper was a quitclaim.

If you received a house by quitclaim from a parent or former partner, record it before you do anything else. A sale cannot close cleanly while the last deed in the chain sits in a drawer.

Does a quitclaim deed need an affidavit filed with the county assessor?

For residential property, usually yes. Section 7-38-12.1 NMSA 1978 requires the person presenting a deed for recording on residential property to also file an affidavit with the county assessor within thirty days of the date of filing with the county clerk. Either the transferor, the transferee or their authorized agents may sign it.

The affidavit is limited to the names and mailing addresses of all transferors and transferees, the legal description, the full consideration paid or exchanged along with the terms of the sale and any seller incentives, and the value and description of personal property included in the price. The assessor keeps the original as a confidential record, and the affidavit is not part of the valuation record.

The statute lists many deeds that do not need the affidavit. Among them:

  • A quitclaim deed to quiet title or clear boundary disputes.
  • An instrument between husband and wife, or parent and child, with only nominal actual consideration.
  • An instrument that confirms or corrects a deed already recorded.
  • A deed from a sale for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • An instrument delivered to establish a gift or a distribution from an estate or trust.

The Santa Fe County Clerk adds a related duty. The clerk sends the assessor a copy of every recorded document, but the person receiving the property is responsible for notifying the assessor so the right person gets the tax bill. Unpaid property tax can eventually lead to a tax sale.

How do tax sale deeds compare with quitclaim deeds?

The New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department says the deed it issues after a delinquent tax auction is equivalent to a quitclaim deed. The deed conveys all of the former owner's interest as of the date the state's lien for real property taxes arose, subject only to perfected interests that existed before that date. The department also states that New Mexico warrants no title to property sold at its auctions.

The department explains that an interest is perfected when the deed or lien is recorded with the county clerk where the property is located. Its guidance adds that the tax deed can be used as the basis to begin clearing title through the court.

Annotations to the Property Tax Code add that grantees under a quitclaim deed from a tax sale purchaser take subject to defects they knew about, or that the record would have shown. The department's delinquent property tax auction page sets out the terms.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When does a quitclaim deed work for selling a New Mexico house, and when does it fall short?

A quitclaim deed works when everyone involved understands that only the signer's actual interest is changing hands. It falls short when a buyer expects promises the form does not contain.

It usually works for:

  • Moving a house between family members who know the history of the property.
  • Removing a former spouse or co-owner who agrees to give up their share.
  • Passing along an inherited house where the heirs have settled who owns what, and the paperwork needs to catch up.

It usually falls short when:

  • The seller wants the buyer to rely on a promise that the title is free of claims.
  • Co-owners or a spouse have not signed, so part of the interest never moved.
  • Liens, unpaid property tax or an old mortgage remain on record.
  • The house is occupied by someone with a claim, such as a tenant or relative, that the deed does not address.

A quitclaim can move an interest quickly, but it cannot make a lien, a missing co-owner or a tax debt disappear. Those items stay with the property, and a buyer's title review will find them. Cash Home Buyers does not promise a price in advance, and each New Mexico house gets looked at on its own facts.

More questions about New Mexico Quitclaim Deed

Is a New Mexico quitclaim deed the same as a warranty deed?

No. The statutory warranty deed form in 47-1-44 NMSA 1978 ends with warranty covenants, and the quitclaim form carries none. A quitclaim transfers only the interest the signer holds.

How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in New Mexico?

The statutory fee is $25 per document under 14-8-15 NMSA 1978. An extra $25 applies for each additional block of ten or fewer index entries beyond the first ten. E-recording vendors add their own convenience fee.

Does a quitclaim deed have to be notarized?

For recording, yes in practice. The Santa Fe County Clerk will not accept a document without a proper notary block. Case annotations under 14-9-3 note that an acknowledgment is not essential to a deed's validity between the parties, but an unrecorded deed can lose to a later good faith buyer.

Can one spouse sign a quitclaim deed alone in New Mexico?

Generally no for community real property. Section 40-3-13 says a transfer by one spouse alone is void, except a direct transfer to the other spouse. A recorded power of attorney or a later written ratification can change the result.

Do I file anything with the county assessor after recording a quitclaim deed?

Often yes for residential property. An affidavit is due to the assessor within thirty days of filing with the clerk under 7-38-12.1, unless an exemption applies, such as a quitclaim to quiet title or a transfer between parent and child for nominal consideration.

Can I sell a house I received by quitclaim deed?

Yes, you can sell whatever interest you hold. The buyer and the title company will review the chain of title, and anything the deed did not clear, such as liens or an unsigned co-owner, will surface at that point.

What law governs a transfer on death deed in New Mexico?

New Mexico transfer on death deeds are governed by the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act, found at 45-6-401 and following in the Uniform Probate Code. Section 45-6-405 NMSA 1978 states the basic rule in one sentence: an individual may transfer property to one or more beneficiaries, effective at the transferor's death, by a transfer on death deed.

The act took effect on January 1, 2014. Under 45-6-403 it applies to a transfer on death deed made before, on or after that date, as long as the transferor dies on or after January 1, 2014. The New Mexico Courts self-help guide, quoted elsewhere on this page, says these deeds have been available since June 2001. The statute and the court guide describe two different dates, and we point to the statute for the rules that apply today.

Section 45-6-404 adds that the act does not displace any other lawful way of passing property in New Mexico. A will, joint tenancy and a trust all remain available, and a transfer on death deed is one tool among them.

What must a New Mexico transfer on death deed contain?

The deed must look like an ordinary recordable deed, say that the transfer happens at death, and be recorded before the owner dies. Section 45-6-409 lists three requirements:

  • It contains the essential elements and formalities of a properly recordable inter vivos deed.
  • It states that the transfer to the designated beneficiary is to occur at the transferor's death.
  • It is recorded before the transferor's death in the office of the county clerk for the county where the property is located.

The recording step is the one people miss. A signed deed in a desk drawer does nothing. Because the deed has to be recorded with the clerk, the recording fee in 14-8-15 NMSA 1978 applies. That section sets the fee at $25 for each document recorded, with extra charges for large documents with many index entries.

Section 45-6-410 removes several steps that people expect. The deed does not require notice to the beneficiary, delivery to the beneficiary, acceptance by the beneficiary during the owner's life, or consideration. The owner can sign and record without telling the person named.

What can the owner still do after recording the deed?

Almost everything. During the owner's life, 45-6-412 says a transfer on death deed does not affect any interest or right of the transferor, including the right to transfer or encumber the property. An owner who has recorded one can still sell the house, refinance it or take out a loan against it.

The same section lists what the deed does not do while the owner is alive:

  • It does not affect the rights of a buyer, even one who knows about the deed.
  • It does not affect the rights of secured or unsecured creditors, current or future.
  • It does not affect the owner's or the beneficiary's eligibility for any form of public assistance.
  • It does not give the beneficiary a legal or equitable interest.
  • It does not expose the property to claims of the beneficiary's creditors.

For a homeowner who wants to sell, this is the key point. The beneficiary named in the deed cannot block a sale, and a buyer does not need the beneficiary's signature. The deed only takes effect if the owner still holds the property at death.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How can a transfer on death deed be changed or revoked?

Only by a new recorded instrument. Under 45-6-411, a revocation works only if it is acknowledged by the transferor after the acknowledgment of the deed being revoked, and recorded before the transferor's death in the county clerk's office where the deed is recorded. It must also take one of three forms: a new transfer on death deed that revokes the earlier one expressly or by inconsistency, an instrument that expressly revokes it, or a regular deed that expressly revokes it.

Two further rules prevent shortcuts. After a transfer on death deed is recorded, it cannot be revoked by a revocatory act on the deed itself, so tearing up a copy or writing across it does nothing. And if the deed was made by more than one owner, a revocation by one does not affect the others, while a deed of joint owners is revoked only if all living joint owners revoke it.

The New Mexico Courts self-help guide says the owner can revoke or amend without the beneficiary's consent or knowledge. That matches the statute, with the recording condition above.

What happens at the owner's death, and who gets the house?

If the named beneficiary survives the owner, the property passes to that beneficiary under the deed. Section 45-6-413 sets out the rest of the rules:

  • A beneficiary who does not survive the owner takes nothing, and that interest lapses.
  • Several beneficiaries take equal, undivided shares with no right of survivorship.
  • If one of several beneficiaries lapses, the others take that share in proportion to their interests.
  • If the owner was a joint owner who is survived by another joint owner, the property belongs to the survivor under the right of survivorship. The deed works only if the owner was the last surviving joint owner.
  • The beneficiary takes subject to all recorded conveyances, mortgages, liens and other recorded interests that exist at the owner's death.
  • The transfer is made without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed says otherwise.

The court guide describes the beneficiary's practical step: file a copy of the death certificate with the county clerk where the real estate is located, after which title passes without probate.

Does the beneficiary owe the owner's debts?

Possibly, to a limited extent. Section 45-6-415 says a beneficiary of a transfer on death deed is liable for an allowed claim against the transferor's probate estate, and for statutory allowances to a surviving spouse and children, to the extent provided in 45-6-102 NMSA 1978.

The deed therefore avoids a probate filing for the house itself but does not make the house untouchable. A mortgage stays attached, and a beneficiary who plans to keep the property still has to keep up payments. Recorded liens also travel with the house, as 45-6-413 states.

The probate court rules say much the same from the estate side. They describe the probate estate as generally excluding property that passes automatically to a listed beneficiary, and they include land subject to transfer on death deeds in that group.

How do transfer on death deeds compare with other routes?

The right route depends on what the owner wants to control. The table summarizes what the sources say for each.

RouteWhat the source saysSource
Transfer on death deedRecorded before death; revocable by recorded instrument; beneficiary gets no interest during the owner's life45-6-409, 45-6-411, 45-6-412
ProbateMay be filed in the probate court of the county where the person lived, between 5 days and 3 years after death; filing cost $30NM Courts self-help guide
Small estate affidavitApplies to estates under $50,000 without real property, after 30 days if no probate is openNM Courts self-help guide
Personal representative's deedMay be needed to move real property out of the decedent's name when the estate includes itNM Courts self-help guide

The self-help guide at selfrepresentation.nmcourts.gov explains probate steps in plain language, and the statute text for 45-6-413 is short enough to read in full.

What if you want to sell a house that has a transfer on death deed?

The answer depends on whether the owner is alive. An owner who is alive can sell as usual, because the deed does not limit the right to transfer. A sale closes with the owner's own signature. Once the owner no longer holds the property at death, the deed has nothing left to transfer.

After an owner dies, the beneficiary has to establish ownership of record first by filing the death certificate with the county clerk. Selling comes next. A buyer will see the recorded deed, the death certificate and any recorded liens in the chain of title. Because the deed passes the house without warranty, the beneficiary should expect the buyer to review the title closely.

Inherited houses often come with repairs, back taxes or relatives who live far away. A cash sale can shorten the process, but it does not change the rules above. Cash Home Buyers makes no price promises in advance, and the beneficiary should confirm title steps with an attorney or title company before signing a contract.

More questions about New Mexico Transfer on Death Deed

Does a New Mexico transfer on death deed avoid probate?

For the house itself, yes, according to the New Mexico Courts guide: the beneficiary files a copy of the death certificate with the county clerk and title passes without probate. The beneficiary can still be liable for allowed claims against the probate estate under 45-6-415.

Must the deed be recorded before the owner dies?

Yes. Section 45-6-409 requires recording before the transferor's death in the office of the county clerk where the property is located.

Does the beneficiary have to be told about the deed?

No. Section 45-6-410 says no notice, delivery or acceptance by the beneficiary is needed during the owner's life, and no consideration is required.

Can the owner sell the house after signing a transfer on death deed?

Yes. Under 45-6-412 the deed does not affect the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property, and the beneficiary has no legal or equitable interest while the owner is alive.

What happens if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

The beneficiary's interest lapses under 45-6-413. If there were several beneficiaries, the surviving ones take the lapsed share in proportion to their interests.

Does a transfer on death deed come with a warranty of title?

No. Section 45-6-413 says the deed transfers property without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed contains a contrary provision.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Mexico Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the New Mexico Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Mexico House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Mexico?
We buy New Mexico houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How does probate work in New Mexico?

New Mexico runs probate under the Uniform Probate Code, Chapter 45 of the state statutes, and cases are filed with the county probate court where the person lived at death. The state court system includes 33 county probate courts alongside 34 district courts, according to the New Mexico Courts website.

The court guide for people without a lawyer says a probate can be filed anywhere from 5 days to 3 years after death, with a filing cost of $30. When there is a will, the court appoints the person named in it as personal representative, also called the executor. The document that gives that authority is called Letters Testamentary. With no will, the same authority comes in Letters of Administration.

For someone inheriting a house, the main question is who has authority to sign a deed. The answer depends on how the house was titled and whether a court has appointed anyone.

Which situations skip probate for a house?

Probate is not needed for real estate held in joint tenancy or with a recorded Transfer on Death Deed, according to the court guide. A surviving spouse can also transfer a community property home titled only in the deceased spouse's name by affidavit, filed six months after the death.

The small estate shortcut usually does not help with a house. A small estate is one worth less than $50,000 that does not include real property, and the successor can collect property using an Affidavit of Successor in Interest once 30 days have passed and no probate has been filed. Land, a house or a farm takes the estate outside that rule.

SituationProbate needed?Detail
Estate under $50,000, no real propertyNoAffidavit of Successor in Interest after 30 days, signed and notarized
Home held in joint tenancyNoPer the NM Courts guide
Home with a recorded Transfer on Death DeedNoPer the NM Courts guide
Community property home in deceased spouse's name onlyNo, with affidavitSurviving spouse files six months after death
Home in the decedent's sole nameUsually yesPersonal representative may need to sign a Personal Representative's deed

Who can act as personal representative?

New Mexico sets a priority order for appointment in Section 45-3-203. The person named in a probated will comes first, followed by the surviving spouse who is also a devisee, other devisees, the surviving spouse, other heirs, and, forty-five days after death, any creditor.

Someone with priority can nominate another qualified person by a signed writing filed with the court, and anyone of age can renounce. A person under the age of majority or found unsuitable in formal proceedings cannot serve. An objection to an appointment can be made only in formal proceedings.

This matters for a sale when several siblings share an inherited house. If they disagree about who serves, the court can step in, and nobody should sign a contract until the appointment is settled.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What does a personal representative do?

The personal representative gathers and inventories assets, notifies heirs, pays debts as far as estate funds allow, distributes the rest under the will or intestacy law and closes the case. The court guide says a case must stay open at least three months before it can be closed, by a sworn statement that the duties are complete.

The representative may not use estate funds for personal benefit but is entitled to fair compensation for time spent. Estate money can pay costs such as postage, filing fees and copies. The guide recommends keeping a written record of tasks and time.

  • Obtain Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration before dealing with the house.
  • Locate the deed, mortgage statements and property tax bills.
  • Keep the property insured and the taxes current while the estate is open.
  • Keep a written log of work and expenses for the court and the heirs.

Who owns the house while probate is open?

Under Section 45-3-101, a person's separate property and share of community property devolves at death to the people named in the will, or to heirs if there is no will. Appellate decisions noted under the statute say real estate passes directly to heirs or devisees and not to the executor.

That ownership is still subject to administration, creditor rights and allowances. The surviving spouse's half of community property stays open to administration until the time to present claims has run, and after that only to the extent needed to pay community claims.

If the estate includes real property, the court guide says the representative may need to execute a Personal Representative's deed to move the property out of the decedent's name. The guide warns that deeds are tricky to draft and suggests hiring an attorney for that step.

How do creditor claims affect a sale?

A personal representative may publish a notice to creditors once a week for three successive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation in the county. Creditors then have four months from the first publication to present claims or be barred, under Section 45-3-801.

Known creditors can also receive written notice by mail or other delivery, and their deadline is the later of four months after publication or sixty days after the notice is delivered. The statute says the representative is not liable to anyone for giving or failing to give this notice, but a 1977 decision cited in the annotations held that publication of the hearing on a final account was not enough notice for known tort claimants.

For heirs planning to sell, this gives a rough timeline, since the claims window runs at least four months from the first publication.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes, unless the will or a court order restricts it. Section 45-3-715 authorizes a representative acting reasonably for the benefit of interested persons to dispose of an asset, including land in New Mexico, for cash or on credit, at public or private sale.

The same section lets the representative make ordinary or extraordinary repairs, insure the assets, pay taxes and assessments and enter leases that extend past the period of administration. If part of the price is on credit, security is required for the unpaid balance unless the district court waives it for good cause.

  • A cash sale avoids the credit and security question altogether.
  • A sale as is can save the estate the cost of repairs, which the statute allows but does not require.
  • The estate can pay property taxes and insurance while the house is on the market.
  • If heirs disagree, a formal proceeding gives the court a role in resolving it.

Cash Home Buyers buys inherited houses in New Mexico as they are. We are not attorneys, and the personal representative should confirm authority with the estate's lawyer before accepting any offer.

What are the time limits and tax issues?

Most informal or formal probate proceedings cannot start more than three years after death, though Section 45-3-108 lists exceptions. One allows a later appointment if no proceedings have happened in the three years, but the representative then has limited rights to possess estate assets and claims other than administration expenses cannot be presented.

Property tax keeps running during probate. Taxes on real property are a lien from January 1 of the tax year, first in priority, under Section 7-38-48. Installments are due November 10 and April 10, and unpaid tax draws interest of one percent a month starting thirty days after the due date.

The assessed value of a house is capped at three percent annual growth, but a change of ownership resets it. The definition of change of ownership in Section 7-36-21.2 excludes some transfers, including a transfer to a child who lives in the home as a principal residence. A sale to an outside buyer is a change of ownership, so the buyer's bill can differ from the one the estate paid.

More questions about New Mexico Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house in New Mexico?

Usually yes if the house was in the decedent's sole name. Probate is not needed when the home was held in joint tenancy or had a recorded Transfer on Death Deed, and a surviving spouse can use an affidavit for a community property home six months after death.

What is the New Mexico small estate limit?

A small estate is worth less than $50,000 and has no real property. A house takes the estate outside the small estate procedure, so an Affidavit of Successor in Interest will not transfer it.

How long does probate take in New Mexico?

A case must stay open at least three months before it can be closed. Creditors have four months from first publication of the notice to present claims, so many estates run longer than three months.

How much does it cost to open probate in New Mexico?

The court guide lists a filing cost of $30. Attorney fees, publication costs and the personal representative's compensation are separate expenses the estate may pay.

What is the deadline to open a New Mexico probate?

A probate can be filed between 5 days and 3 years after death. After three years, only limited proceedings are allowed under Section 45-3-108.
